title: Evaluating Test-Time Scaling of General LLM Agents
claim: Agents lose substantial performance in realistic general settings, and neither longer interaction nor more sampling reliably recovers it.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: radar chart, line plot, gap-shaded curve plot
description: A three-panel figure with a caption under each panel. (a) is a radar chart labeled GPT-5 at its center. A gray octagon shows the standard setting, and a red inner polygon shows the general setting. Axes are benchmarks such as MathHay, MCP-Bench, SWE-Bench, Terminal-Bench, BrowseComp, Mind2-Web2 and Web-voyager. Red labels with down arrows give percentage drops, from 6% to 58%. (b) plots success rate against interaction turns. A dashed blue line shows expected linear growth. A red line shows actual performance, which rises, reaches an orange 'Scaling Plateau' marker, then fluctuates and declines. (c) plots accuracy against number of samples K. A green upper-bound curve sits well above purple, orange and red curves for Majority Vote, Self-Choice and Pairwise. The green shaded area between them is labeled 'Verifiability Gap'. Red and orange text highlights the key points.
caption: Main contribution of this paper. A: GPT-5's performance drop under General AgentBench compared to domain-specific evaluation. B: Sequential test-time scaling via longer interaction turns out to be unstable or to degrade performance. C: Agents fail to utilize the improvement brought by multiple sampling due to verification gap.
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly expected to operate as general-purpose systems that resolve real-world user requests, yet their dynamic scaling behavior in realistic environments remains poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate two principal test-time scaling axes of LLM agents: sequential scaling through extended interaction and parallel scaling through trajectory sampling. We first introduce a realistic benchmark that provides one unified framework for evaluating LLM agents across search, coding, reasoning, and tool-use domains, more faithfully reflecting the heterogeneity of real-world deployments. Evaluating ten leading LLM agents reveals substantial performance degradation when transitioning from domain-specific evaluations to this realistic setting. Building on this foundation, we progressively scale test-time compute along fine-grained increments to characterize the performance upper bound. We find that neither scaling axis can consistently yield meaningful gains from additional test-time compute in realistic environments, a phenomenon we attribute to two fundamental limitations: the scaling plateau that bottlenecks sequential scaling and the verification gap that undermines parallel scaling. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/cxcscmu/General-AgentBench.
